2.text: a storehouse in order to sell them to the whalers. The skins were restored

3.text: to their owner, but the thief was not punished, except with harsh words. As

4.text: witnessed by Nordenskiöld, theft, and deceit toward a stranger, are not considered

5.text: unlawful. I must acknowledge, however, that, during my journey among the

6.text: Maritime Chukchee and the Eskimo, hardly any of my belongings were lost;

7.text: while among the Reindeer people not a single trip would pass without almost

8.text: open attempts at stealing, amounting even to robbery. “Look out for my

9.text: mother!” I was once warned by my host. “Her nature is such, that she

10.text: will steal even fresh excrement from under a man.”

11.text: Among the Reindeer people, indeed, theft between the camps and herds

12.text: is held to be an almost lawful pursuit. There is in the language, besides the

13.text: usual word for stealing, tɪ-tuleˊerkɪn (“I steal”), still another, rather euphemistic

14.text: term, tɪ-ng̣ɪntɪweˊerkɪn (“I abstract;” literally, “I cause [the thing] to flee”).

15.text: Quarrels are continually going on between neighbors on account of mutual

16.text: accusations. Several of the people that I knew were given new derisive names

17.text: on account of their thieving exploits. One was called “Knee-Walker” (Ñɪreˊ-

18.text: čeiˊvun) because he was once accused of crawling on all-fours to his neighbor’s

19.text: herd in the calving-season with the intention of taking away some of the new-

20.text: born fawns. Another was called “Necklaced Latuˊwg̣ê” (Êˊnnɪčhɪ-Latuˊᵋwg̣ê)
20.note: that rarest of birds, a typesetter mistake

21.text: because while on a visit to another camp he stole some half-cooked entrails

22.text: that were boiling in the kettle, wound them around his neck, and, when pursued,

23.text: continued to eat from one end thereof. These names stick so well, that at

24.text: last even the persons themselves begin to use them, especially after some

25.text: trouble with the spirits of disease, when the Chukchee like to change their

26.text: names. During the Russian fairs small thefts take place every day in the

27.text: block-houses as well as in the camps, and even inside the tents. In my

28.text: presence, a young man who came into the trading-store, picked up a bunch

29.text: of squirrel-skins from the floor, and tried to sell them to their real owner.

30.text: When detected, he only said, “Take them, if they are yours,” and then sat

31.text: down on the bench, waiting for the usual hospitality.¹ I have in my collection

32.text: a white fox-skin roughly patched with hare-skin to make it look whole. Norden-

33.text: skiöld² relates similar tricks, chiefly of the Arctic Maritime Chukchee.

34.text: As mentioned before, quarrelling between the Chukchee and their neigh-

35.text: bors has almost ceased. The Kerek of Cape Barykoff occasionally complain

36.text: that the Telqäˊp Chukchee ill-treat them, taking their peltries without paying

37.text: for them, and carrying away their children to use as herdsmen; but even

38.text: here a good mutual understanding usually prevails, since the Kerek obtain

39.text: from the Telqäˊp Chukchee reindeer-skins for garments, sinew for nets, meat,

40.text: Russian wares, and American rifles and cartridges, which come all the way
